absent: No critical, feminist or decolonial scholarship, no education-research literature on teaching critical thinking, and nothing on professional judgement — though the paper generalises about educators and students.
forYou: An unusually short lineage for an argument about professional judgement: Dewey plus three recent psychology sources. Next to your Professional Criticality reading, the missing middle is what stands out.
method: References from the paper; strands and narrative by Claude, grounded only in that list.
narrative: The paper's root is Dewey (1910, 1933): critical thinking as careful, reflective consideration of belief. That definition is quoted in the first endnote and carries the whole argument.

Its debate is the old one about whether thinking can be taught on its own. McPeck (1981) said no; Bailin et al. (1999) tried to conceptualise the field. Kirkham sides with stand-alone teaching and leaves the debate in a footnote.

The virtue turn comes from McGilchrist (2021), whose distinction between rationality and reason underwrites the closing conception. The empirical layer is thin and recent: David et al. (2024) on the unpleasantness of mental effort, Haidt (2024) on adolescent anxiety, Gerlich (2025) on cognitive offloading.
